data.title: Is functional integration of resting state brain networks an unspecific biomarker for working memory performance?
data.text:
Connectivity analysis and network constructionParcellation scheme
To subdivide the brain in different subregions the parcellation routine from Fornito et al. (2010) andZalesky et al. (2010) was applied.
This approach randomly parcellates the anatomically delineated and labelled T1 volume provided by the AAL toolbox in SPM ( TzourioMazoyer et al., 2002 ) into a number of cortical regions (in our case
462 regions). In contrast to other approaches, this parcellation has the
advantage of generating similar-sized brain parcels. Thus, if time series
are averaged across voxels within a parcel, mean time series are equallyaffected by noise and are equally reliable. To document that our results
on both global and nodal levels can be reproduced when a different
parcellation scheme is employed ( Craddock et al., 2012 )w ea d d e df u r -
ther analyses in the Supplementary material (see Inline SupplementaryTables S1 and S3, Inline Supplementary Fig. S1).
Inline Supplementary Tables S1 and S3, Fig. S1 can be found online at
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.12.046 .

In order to minimize the effects of spurious temporal correlations induced by physiological and movement artefacts the six rigid-body
movement parameters from the realignment procedure and two additional mean time series extracted from areas within white-matter and
ventricles were regressed out from the local time series. It has been
previously shown that the behavioural correlates of the brain functional
network topology are best observed in the frequency range below
0.1 Hz ( Achard et al., 2006 ). Therefore regional time series were bandpass filtered by means of maximum overlap discrete wavelet transform
(MODWT; Percival and Walden, 2006 ) within four frequency intervals
(in the range of 0.02 –0.33 Hz, each corresponding to a wavelet scale).
As the result of our analysis of functional connectivity revealed the
strongest difference in correlations between mean connectivity and
each the CS and the SWM task in wavelet scale 2 (see scale 2 (0.08 –0.17 Hz). The behavioural relevance of this frequency
range was also documented in our previous work. In Giessing et al.
(2013) we found that experimentally induced changes in performance predominately correlated with changes in functional connectivity in the same frequency components. In order to obtain a
measure of association between each pair of cortical regions, Pearson
correlation between wavelet coef ficients were computed which in
turn gave an NbyNassociation matrix ( Ndenotes the number of
nodes) for the resting state data set of each subject. The global
strength of functional connectivity was estimated by computing
the mean of each association matrix.

Networks were constructed at 16 equally spaced connection densities (cost thresholds), in the range of 5% –50%. The connection density
reflects the percentage of edges in a graph and is de fined as the number
of edges in the graph relative to the maximum possible number of edges
((N×(N−1) / 2) where Nequals the number of nodes). Binary graphs
at each arbitrary connection density were constructed by thresholdingeach association matrix to create an adjacency matrix. Binary instead
of weighted graphs were used in order to disentangle differences in
network densities from differences in topology ( Ginestet et al., 2011 ).
The above thresholding was implemented by means of an algorithmwhich is based on the minimum spanning tree of a graph. This algorithm ensures that all regional nodes are connected by at least one
edge to the rest of the network, even at the sparsest connection density
(Alexander-Bloch et al., 2010 ). Once the minimum spanning tree was
detected, edges were rank thresholded and added in the order of their absolute correlation strength.

Network diagnostics
To analyse network integration on different organizational levels
three key topological properties were estimated for each graph at
each connection density ( Latora and Marchiori, 2001 ): network efficiency, modularity and clustering. For each topological property we computed a global network metric which characterizes the topological
property at the whole brain scale (global scale) and a regional metric
characterizing the same property but for a certain brain node (nodal
scale).

Modularity

sub-networks which are relatively densely intra-connected, and relatively sparsely interconnected. To estimate modularity resting state networks were decomposed into non-overlapping modules by maximizing
the modularity index Q(Newman, 2006 ) through the Louvain algorithm
available from Brain Connectivity Toolbox ( Blondel et al., 2008; Rubinov
and Sporns, 2010 ).

Clustering
To estimate the integration of nodes surrounding a certain node we
computed the clustering coef ficient for each node iof the network. The
clustering coef ficient of node iis equal to the ratio L/T, where Lis the
number of edges between nodes that are directly connected with
node i,a n d Tis the number of edges that could possibly exist between
these nearest neighbours of node i(Watts and Strogatz, 1998 ). This
can be averaged over all nodes to estimate the clustering of the graph
as a whole. Thus networks that have a cliquish organization, characterized by many connections between the nearest neighbours of any given
node, will have high clustering.

Controlling effects of network densities
To show that our results are stable across different network densities
we used two different approaches for the analyses on the global scale. In
thefirst approach we performed statistical tests on equally spaced
sampling points within the investigated range of network density. Inthe second approach we averaged graph metrics across the entire
range of network density to avoid multiple comparisons at individual
sampling points and to reduce the dependency of any signi ficant differences in network topology on the arbitrary choice of a single connectiondensity. This approach has been used in previous graph analyses
(Bassett et al., 2008; Lynall et al., 2010; Giessing et al., 2013 ) and its theoretical background was discussed in detail by Ginestet et al. (2011) .
